I have some questions on the new traffic devices on Brookview Drive  

I’m not sure what to call them  I appreciate the intent and the need to slow people down. Maybe the devices closer to the intersection with Kenore need to be tweaked, though.

Today I was coming down the hill on my bike and nearing the devices. A car came up the hill, driving fast, and didn’t slow down going through the devices. It continued driving fast afterwards. I was able to slow down and pass through the devices after it got past. If we had been a couple of seconds closer though, I would have had to go into the devices or the curb to avoid being hit by the car. I could have been badly injured. 

Observations:
- The devices don’t make cars slow down — they’re suggestive, and not everyone will take the suggestion.
- Located where they are, they are potentially hazardous for cyclists. The steep hill adds a lot of speed quickly. 
- Visibility to oncoming traffic is limited by the foliage, so reaction time is limited.

Could the devices be relocated further down the hill and closer to Kenmore? The slope isn’t so steep there, and visibility is better. Perhaps they should be put a little further out into the road as well to make it narrower so cars are more likely to slow down.

Thanks for considering this.

properties.description:
Tonya Miltier, 801 Churchill Dr, Chapel Hill
Stormwater Issue
There is increasing erosion of my property along the Town of Chapel Hill stormwater easement and piping that runs through my backyard. The Town’s easement, large pipe, ongoing stormwater flow, significant undercutting and bank erosion, and easement construction are all contributors to this problem:

1.	There is a large stormwater pipe running through the backyard. The discharge of this pipe is located about ¾ of the way through the yard where it then opens into a free-running ditch.  This pipe drains a significant area of the neighborhood through the backyard.  During rainstorms there is a large amount of water flowing through the pipe, outlet, and drainage, and large amounts of water run in a constant stream for 24-48+ hours after a rain even if surrounding areas are completely dry.
2.	The Town of Chapel Hill appears to have a 15 ft easement on the property that encompasses the entire pipe and eroded area.
3.	There is significant erosion and undercutting of the bank – and into the yard - and the erosion is extending significantly beyond the rocks currently at the sides of the outflow of the pipe.
4.	Without some kind of remedial measures and repair the stormwater outflows will continue to accelerate the erosion of the 4-5 foot bank and begin to encroach beyond the Town of Chapel Hill easement into the rest of the yard.  The undercutting erosion process is also creating a safety hazard as part of the bank appears solid from above, but is actually hollow underneath.

I’m requesting that the Town of Chapel Hill come and inspect the easement, bank, pipe outflow, and current erosion and create a plan to mitigate the current damage and to prepare the pipe, outflow and bank for the more frequent severe storms we are experiencing here in town so damage doesn’t continue.
